title: Leslies House

jokes.text: Teacher reveals her class is called 'Coping with Terminal Illness' in response to Leslie's cheerful advice to make students leave with a smile.
jokes.setup: Leslie cheerfully tells the teachers to make sure their students leave with a smile to boost evaluations.
jokes.punchline: One teacher flatly announces her class is 'Coping with Terminal Illness,' undercutting the pep-talk completely.
jokes.explanation: The joke is beautifully structured: Leslie's sunny bureaucratic optimism ('leave with a smile') collides perfectly with the darkest possible class subject. The punchline lands hard because it's the most extreme logical counterexample. Economy is excellent — the class name alone does all the work.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: These recreation classes are jewels in Pawnee's beautiful crown.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Unfortunately, due to budget cuts, we're going to have to eliminate them all.

jokes.text: 'Hopefully your attendance is good!' / 'Actually, no, hopefully it's bad.'
jokes.setup: Leslie reflexively tries to recover with an optimistic comment about attendance.
jokes.punchline: She immediately self-corrects, realizing high attendance at a terminal illness coping class is actually terrible news.
jokes.explanation: A tight double-beat that extends joke 1. Leslie's instinct to be positive, then the dawning horror of what she just said, is perfectly timed. The self-correction shows smart character integration — Leslie is too earnest not to catch her own mistake, which is funnier than just letting it sit.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Make sure the students leave with a smile.

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.line: My class is about terminal illness.

jokes.text: Leslie's talking-head about learning 'hair braiding, biscuits, and French kissing' at rec center classes — 'The French kissing was just from a boy in my biscuits class, but either way, lesson learned.'
jokes.setup: Leslie lists the valuable life skills she gained from rec center classes, building to what sounds like a legitimate class.
jokes.punchline: French kissing was not a class — it was a boy in her biscuits class — but she treats the incidental encounter as equally educational.
jokes.explanation: This is classic Leslie Knope character comedy. The joke only works because of who she is: someone who earnestly treats every experience as a learning opportunity. The matter-of-fact 'either way, lesson learned' is the kicker that elevates it from a simple misdirection into deep character work. High quotability and rewatch value.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay everyone, I want to encourage perfect attendance at all our classes. Perfect attendance shows dedication and responsibility.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait... except for the terminal illness class. You know what? Bad attendance is fine there. In fact, I'm gonna say skipping that one is encouraged.

jokes.text: Justin mentions a fish reminds him of his mom. 'Why?' 'It's just being really withholding.'
jokes.setup: Justin says a fish at the aquarium reminds him of his mom, a seemingly sweet or random observation.
jokes.punchline: The reason is that his mom is 'really withholding,' delivered casually as if this is a completely normal thing to say.
jokes.explanation: Elegant misdirection and genuine wit. The audience expects something charming or poetic about the fish; instead they get a quick, dark psychological portrait of Justin's mother. The deadpan delivery makes it funnier than if it were played for shock. High originality for a throwaway line.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We offered French kissing, salsa dancing, pottery...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Actually, the French kissing wasn't an official class. That was just a boy in the biscuits class.

jokes.text: Justin reveals the exotic food is camel stomach, then immediately backtracks — 'I'm teasing, it's chicken' — then offers actual camel stomach.
jokes.setup: Leslie tries the food and loves it; Justin says it's camel stomach.
jokes.punchline: He immediately says he's joking — it's chicken — then casually asks if she'd like to try the actual camel stomach, implying it's also on the table.
jokes.explanation: A competent two-beat joke. The first beat (camel stomach reveal) is predictable, but the second beat — that the camel stomach is a separate, real option — is a nice escalation that salvages it. Works as character establishment for Justin as a worldly adventurer.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Because the fish is being withholding

jokes.text: Leslie's talking-head: 'I've racked my brain and I can't come up with one exciting idea.'
jokes.setup: Leslie just confidently told Justin their Pawnee date would 'blow Indianapolis out of the water.'
jokes.punchline: Immediately cut to Leslie admitting she has absolutely no ideas whatsoever.
jokes.explanation: A well-executed juxtaposition cut — the mockumentary format at its most functional. Leslie's confident promise immediately undercut by her panicked confessional. Structure does the heavy lifting here; the joke itself is conventional but lands because of the editing rhythm.

dialogue.speaker: Justin
dialogue.line: Try some of this camel stomach.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Camel stomach? Really?

dialogue.speaker: Justin
dialogue.line: I'm just kidding, it's chicken.

jokes.text: Ann suggests a simple one-on-one dinner; Leslie immediately hijacks it into a 'big rambling party' and calls their lunches 'think tanks.'
jokes.setup: Ann offers the sensible, modest suggestion: just cook him chicken at home.
jokes.punchline: Leslie transforms it into an elaborate dinner party and credits Ann's 'genius,' then reframes their lunches as 'think tanks' in the same breath.
jokes.explanation: Strong character integration — Leslie's pattern of taking someone else's idea and immediately inflating it beyond recognition is core to who she is. The 'think tank' non-sequitur at the end is a nice bonus absurdist beat. Slightly bloated in delivery but the character work is genuine.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Pawnee is going to blow Indianapolis out of the water. Our date night is going to be so much better than theirs.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I have no idea what we're doing.

jokes.text: Justin once ate fried cockatoo with a member of the Thai Royal Family
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to think of exciting things to do in Pawnee to impress Justin
jokes.punchline: Her benchmark for 'impressive' is that he once ate fried cockatoo with Thai royalty — an impossible standard for Pawnee to meet
jokes.explanation: Works as world-building comedy — the specificity of 'fried cockatoo' and 'Thai Royal Family' together is absurdly perfect. Functional joke that establishes the episode's central tension (Pawnee vs. Justin's exotic life) economically.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Justin ate fried cockatoo with Thai royalty.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Why don't you just make up an exotic dish with a local bird name? Like fried Indiana pigeon or something?

jokes.text: A dinner party! That's genius... No, I actually meant more like a one-on-one thing. / I know what you meant, but I took your idea and I made it better. / It's called a think tank, Ann.
jokes.setup: Ann suggests something intimate; Leslie immediately hijacks it into a large dinner party.
jokes.punchline: Leslie declares she 'made it better' and then non-sequiturs into calling their lunches 'think tanks' as if that's relevant justification.
jokes.explanation: Strong character comedy — Leslie's utter confidence in steamrolling a reasonable suggestion is quintessentially her. 'It's called a think tank, Ann' is a great non-sequitur pivot that only Leslie would make.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Maybe we could have an intimate dinner?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh, that's a great idea! We should throw a dinner party instead!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: See, I improved your idea. It's like how I've improved all your ideas. Remember when we used to have lunch? I turned those into think tanks.

jokes.text: Ron's negotiation about bringing a large number of deviled eggs he doesn't want to share with anyone.
jokes.setup: Leslie is asking about the dinner party logistics.
jokes.punchline: Ron's primary concern is securing personal refrigerator space for a large private deviled egg supply that he has zero intention of sharing.
jokes.explanation: Pure Ron Swanson. The joke is almost entirely in the character integration — only Ron would approach a social gathering with the principal concern of protecting his private food supply from other guests. Delivered with deadpan authority, this lands as both a great joke and a perfect character portrait. High rewatch value.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: How many courses are we talking about here?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, we're starting with seven.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Actually, eight.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Nine, if we count the palate cleanser.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Which we do.

jokes.text: Leslie tells Tom he's being invited because he comes from 'the most distant and exotic land.' Tom: 'South Carolina?'
jokes.setup: Leslie flatters Tom by calling him her most 'exotic' guest, implying a far-flung origin.
jokes.punchline: Tom dryly reveals the 'exotic' land is South Carolina — a completely unremarkable American state.
jokes.explanation: Tight and economical. Leslie's Pawnee-centric worldview makes anyone from outside Indiana 'exotic,' and the reveal of South Carolina is the perfect anti-climax. Tom's dry delivery ('South Carolina?') with implied chagrin is exactly right. Works on multiple levels: Leslie's parochialism and Tom's identity as someone who thinks he's more cosmopolitan than he is.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm bringing a dish to the potluck, but I want to make it very clear that it's not for sharing. It's for me. I'll eat the whole thing right there at the table while you all watch and feel jealous.

jokes.text: Andy is polishing a bench and asks Leslie if he can come to the party. Leslie invites him — to serve coats and food at $10/hour. Andy: 'My guardian angel!'
jokes.setup: Andy seems to be angling for a party invitation; Leslie appears to be extending one.
jokes.punchline: She's actually hiring him as a servant at minimum party wages, and Andy responds with complete, unironic gratitude.
jokes.explanation: The 'My guardian angel!' reaction is what makes this work. Andy's complete earnestness in being grateful for what is objectively a bad deal is deeply funny and character-consistent. The joke rewards the audience's knowledge of Andy's life situation.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom, you're from South Carolina, which is basically the most exotic place anyone could be from.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: South Carolina is hardly exotic.

jokes.text: Andy rehearses being Justin, imagining Justin will say he got his coat 'from the king of Africa when we were walking on the Berlin Wall together.' Then: 'Really, Justin? What instruments do you play?'
jokes.setup: Andy is practicing how to interact with Justin, roleplaying both sides of the conversation.
jokes.punchline: His imagined Justin is so absurdly over-the-top that 'walking on the Berlin Wall together with the king of Africa' is treated as a normal Justin story. The follow-up question about instruments is a non-sequitur punchline.
jokes.explanation: Fun absurdist riff on Justin's worldly reputation. The joke escalates Justin's legend to parody levels, and the non-sequitur follow-up question ('What instruments do you play?') is a chaotic little bonus. Andy's anxious preparation to impress someone who doesn't know he exists is good character work.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Leslie, whatever you do, do not invite Jerry to this.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Hi everybody!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh, Jerry, hey...

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: We were just talking about... um...

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: What were you guys talking about?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Nothing! It's nothing. Hey, shouldn't you be getting home?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, like, right now?

jokes.text: 'Actually, he's a pretty sick keyboardist.' (Talking head response to Andy's question about Justin's instruments, validating the absurd premise)
jokes.setup: Andy's ridiculous roleplayed question about what instruments Justin plays.
jokes.punchline: A talking-head cut reveals someone confirming that Justin actually does play keyboard — making Andy's random guess accidentally correct.
jokes.explanation: The mockumentary cut to a confessional accidentally validating Andy's absurd improv is a structurally elegant joke. The economy is nearly perfect — four words confirm the gag. Rewatch bonus because you look for it the second time. The 'pretty sick' delivery adds casual cool to the confirmation.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm practicing taking coats. This is Justin. He's a professional ice skater who also works as a lifeguard at an indoor pool. He's won three Grammys for yodeling.

jokes.text: Andy tells a customer (Kyle) there might be a stain on his ass right before he sits down on the freshly-polished wet bench, then immediately says 'No, no, you're good.'
jokes.setup: Andy has been polishing benches (and earlier was asked if the polish would get on people's butts). A customer is about to sit down.
jokes.punchline: Andy raises the alarm right as the person sits, then immediately retracts it — suggesting the person now has a polish stain but Andy is too awkward to deal with it.
jokes.explanation: A payoff for the earlier bench-polishing setup. The callback is earned and Andy's characteristically conflict-avoidant 'No, no, you're good' is perfectly in character. Visual gag lands well in context.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Hey! How are you doing? Those benches are looking really shiny, right? I just polished them.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Um, I don't want to be weird, but is that a stain on your butt?

jokes.text: Hi, Kyle. You know, right before you sat down, I noticed, did you have some kind of stain on your ass, or something? What was that? / What? / No, no, no. You're good.
jokes.setup: Andy was just told his freshly polished bench might transfer polish to sitters' butts.
jokes.punchline: A customer sits down and Andy immediately inspects them for polish transfer, pretends to see something alarming, then reassures them — the polish has transferred but Andy covers it up to avoid admitting his error.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback payoff to the polish setup. The visual comedy of Andy inspecting a stranger's butt, the slight alarm, then the cover-up 'No, no, you're good' is well-executed. Physical comedy inferred from context.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I can't believe you've never been over to my house before!

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, now I know why.

jokes.text: Ann's reaction to seeing Leslie's house for the first time: 'Now, I can believe it.' (re: never having been invited over)
jokes.setup: Ann notes she can't believe Leslie has never had her over. Leslie says it's 'a little messy.'
jokes.punchline: After seeing the interior, Ann deadpans that she now completely understands why she's never been invited.
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect economy — five words do all the work. The joke implies rather than shows, trusting the audience to fill in the horror of the house. Ann's dry straight-man energy makes it land. The structure (setup the sweet sentiment, invert it immediately) is clean.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, I found this old newspaper from 1987 while cleaning out the storage closet.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: 1987? That's historical! We have to keep this. This could be important for Pawnee's archives.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: It's just the sports section.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Even better. Sports history IS history.

jokes.text: Ann's talking-head: 'I think I need to call Child Services and have Leslie taken away from herself.'
jokes.setup: Ann is helping Leslie clean the disaster that is her house.
jokes.punchline: Ann frames the situation as child endangerment — with Leslie as both the child and the danger — and proposes an absurd bureaucratic solution.
jokes.explanation: This is genuinely excellent joke writing. The conceit of Leslie needing to be protected from herself via bureaucratic intervention is both absurdist and psychologically true. 'Taken away from herself' is a memorably phrased construction that couldn't be more economical. High quotability — this is the kind of line that gets repeated. Justified 8+ rating: it's original, perfectly structured, and deeply character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, we need to talk about your house. There's pizza boxes from 2009, half-eaten waffles, and what appears to be a nest made of government documents.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann, that's not a nest, that's my filing system.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: You have a Batman costume pinned to your wall and a life-size cardboard cutout of yourself in the corner. When was the last time you cleaned?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I don't have time to clean when there's so much government work to do!

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Okay, here's what's going to happen. I'm taking away your office supplies for a week. And you're going to bed at a reasonable hour. And we're going to work on using your big girl words to express your feelings.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann, I'm a government official.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: You eat ice cream for breakfast and name your waffle maker. You need an intervention.

jokes.text: Ann describes Leslie's house as 'like a crazy person's garage.'
jokes.setup: Ann is confronted with the full chaos of Leslie's home interior.
jokes.punchline: She describes it not as a crazy person's house, but specifically a crazy person's *garage* — implying the house is so disorganized it's like a secondary storage space for a mentally unstable person.
jokes.explanation: A well-chosen simile with good specificity — 'garage' rather than just 'house' does real work. Not groundbreaking but clean and well-delivered.

jokes.text: Leslie spots a newspaper from November 1986 and says 'Oh, the first rumblings of Iran-Contra! Don't throw that out!'
jokes.setup: Ann is trying to throw away obviously outdated newspapers as part of the cleanup.
jokes.punchline: Leslie treats a nearly 30-year-old newspaper as an essential historical document — specifically citing Iran-Contra — and defends keeping it with civic urgency.
jokes.explanation: The Iran-Contra specificity is what makes this joke sing. Any political nerd would hoard newspapers for exactly this reason, and it's perfectly Leslie that she not only has the paper but knows its historical significance off the top of her head. Strong character integration — this joke could only be Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Why do we need two birdhouses?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh, that's simple. One is for birds.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And the other one is for birds.

jokes.text: The birdhouse exchange: 'What do you need this birdhouse for?' / 'I might need it.' / 'What about this one?' / 'Well, if two birds come along?'
jokes.setup: Ann is trying to declutter Leslie's hoarded house and asks about a birdhouse.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's defense is pure contingency-hoarder logic: she might need it. When Ann finds a second one, Leslie escalates: two birds.
jokes.explanation: The escalating hoarder logic is nicely observed and character-specific. 'Well, if two birds come along?' has a good rhythm. Solid mid-tier joke that rewards Leslie's characterization as someone who cannot throw anything away.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Shake my hand.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Why?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Just shake it. I want to see what kind of person you are based on your handshake.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's not a thing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A firm handshake shows confidence. A limp handshake shows weakness.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Or it shows I don't want to touch you.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Just try it.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Fine.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Hmm. Interesting. Very interesting. You have the grip of someone who has definitely thought about hurting people, but chooses not to most days.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Great. Can I go?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, I'm going to tell Justin that your handshake means you're a murderer.

jokes.text: Tom asks April to shake his hand to test if he's exfoliated too much. April: 'Ew! It's like touching raw chicken.' Tom: 'Damn it. Gonna have to re-foliate them.'
jokes.setup: Tom is anxious about making a good impression on Justin and is testing his handshake by having April feel his hand.
jokes.punchline: April's visceral disgust ('like touching raw chicken') and Tom's determined response to 're-foliate' escalates the absurdity.
jokes.explanation: 'Re-foliate' as a made-up word for re-doing the exfoliation is a nice touch. April's disgust is perfectly in character and the raw chicken comparison is memorably gross. Tom's vanity anxiety is well-deployed character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Pawnee is so unhip, we're still mourning Kurt Cobain like he just died yesterday.

jokes.text: Tom's talking-head: 'People in this town are just now getting into Nirvana. I don't have the heart to tell them what's going to happen to Kurt Cobain in 1994.'
jokes.setup: Tom is explaining that Pawnee is unhip and he needs to bone up on his cosmopolitan credentials.
jokes.punchline: He references Pawnee's cultural lag with a darkly funny specific — they're just discovering Nirvana, unaware that Kurt Cobain is already dead (the show is set circa 2010).
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. It works on multiple levels: Pawnee's established backwardness, Tom's condescending compassion, and the dark comedy of treating Kurt Cobain's death as a spoiler to be withheld out of kindness. 'I don't have the heart to tell them' implies a sensitivity he definitely doesn't have. The specificity of '1994' makes it sharper. Justified 8+ — this is genuinely excellent writing that rewards smart viewers.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Your hands are so... textured.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Thank you! I moisturize.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No, like... in a bad way. They're like tree bark.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, I work with my hands. I'm very hands-on.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You need to refoliate them or something.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Refoliate? That's not a word.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: It should be.

jokes.text: April's reaction to shaking Tom's over-exfoliated hand: 'Ew! It's like touching raw chicken.'
jokes.setup: Tom has April shake his hand to evaluate his exfoliation level
jokes.punchline: April's verdict is immediate and visceral: 'It's like touching raw chicken.' Tom resolves to 're-foliate'
jokes.explanation: April's delivery is the whole joke — her disgusted specificity ('raw chicken') and the nonchalance of walking away after. Tom's response ('gonna have to re-foliate') is a made-up word that perfectly caps the absurdity. Strong callback payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.line: I'm offering free tutoring to show the value of this class.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's wonderful! Ron and I would love your help.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Speak for yourself. I don't need tutoring.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, come on. Just give it a try. *winks*

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.line: Yes, Ron, it could really help you. *winks*

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Stop winking at me. Both of you. It's unsettling.

jokes.text: Maria (organizer) keeps winking at Leslie after insisting her help won't influence Leslie's class-cutting decision.
jokes.setup: Maria is helping clean Leslie's house for free and keeps insisting it won't affect Leslie's evaluation of her class.
jokes.punchline: She immediately undercuts every disclaimer with a conspiratorial wink, making the quid pro quo completely obvious.
jokes.explanation: A functional running gag throughout the episode — the teachers' obvious attempts to curry favor while maintaining deniability. The winking is a predictable punchline but works in context. Not original but consistent.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I have planned an amazing five-course meal for tonight.

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.line: What's the first course?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Soup.

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.line: What kind of soup?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: ...Hot soup.

jokes.text: Oh! No, no, I insist on paying. / No, no, I insist on demonstrating. / This is not gonna affect my decision at all. / Oh! Of course not. / Stop winking.
jokes.setup: The organizing teacher has helped clean Leslie's house and Leslie insists on paying; the teacher insists it's a demonstration to save her class.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's repeated 'this won't affect my decision' paired with the teacher's persistent winking makes both parties complicit in a transparent quid pro quo they're both pretending isn't happening.
jokes.explanation: 'Stop winking' is the perfect button — Leslie trying to maintain plausible deniability while the teacher openly signals their arrangement. Good cringe comedy from the mutual pretense.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Your house is cleaner than last time.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Last time? When were you here before?

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: I don't know, a few months ago maybe?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: ...I think you might have me confused with someone else.

jokes.text: The cooking teacher's food is 'a very good sampling of what my level one class does, which I hope you'll keep in mind.' Leslie: 'Tania, like I said over the phone—' Tania: 'I know. It won't influence your decision.'
jokes.setup: Another teacher has shown up to help — this time cooking the dinner party food — while maintaining the fiction that it's not a bribe.
jokes.punchline: The same pattern as Maria: disclaimer followed by obvious self-interest.
jokes.explanation: Third instance of the teacher-bribe running gag. The repetition diminishes the laugh each time, though the structure is still functional. This version adds less than the previous ones.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Wait. Mark was at your place? Before we started dating?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yeah, we were just going over some city planning stuff.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: So you two were alone together. In your apartment. At night.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann, nothing happened. We were just—

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I'm dating a man who has been to your apartment. That's my boyfriend. In your space.

jokes.text: Andy promises not to spit in anyone's food 'unless they should request that I do.'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks if Andy will be okay serving at the party given the complicated guest list (Mark, Justin).
jokes.punchline: Andy's professional assurance includes a bizarre carve-out for consensual food-spitting, delivered with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: The specific phrasing 'unless they should request that I do' is delightfully formal and strange, suggesting Andy has encountered this scenario and thought it through. The contrast between professional language and disgusting premise is excellent. Pure Andy Dwyer character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: So Justin was telling me about this time he went swimming with whale sharks in the Maldives, and I was like, 'That's cool, I once ate a hamburger that was pretty big.'

jokes.text: Mark mentions he's been to Leslie's house before. Leslie: 'You've been here? Right.' Then an awkward beat.
jokes.setup: Mark mentions Leslie's house is cleaner than last time he was there.
jokes.punchline: Leslie hadn't told anyone about their history; the slip causes visible embarrassment and an uncomfortable acknowledgment.
jokes.explanation: A well-handled cringe beat. The pregnant pause after Mark's slip communicates the history without spelling it out. The economy of 'You've been here? Right.' is good — Leslie catching herself and pivoting awkwardly. Works as character drama with a comedic edge.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay everyone, I need to ration out the stories tonight. We have limited inventory. So Ben, you get one story. Ann, you get one story. Tom, you're on a story budget of two, but only if they're good.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What if I want to tell the one about the time I wore those pants that were too tight?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's not happening. That's not a story, that's a cry for help.

jokes.text: Mark's talking-head about Justin: 'Last time he told me about snorkeling with whale sharks in Madagascar. That was after I told him I sometimes go swimming at the Y.'
jokes.setup: Mark is expressing excitement about seeing Justin again.
jokes.punchline: The contrast between Justin's whale shark story and Mark's admission that he goes to the YMCA to swim is a perfect deadpan self-deprecating reveal.
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition is earned and specific. Mark's flat confession about the Y makes the story funnier than any explicit joke about being boring would. The structure — Justin's story, then the reveal of what prompted it — works beautifully. Strong economy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Everyone needs to have fun, but also be extremely quiet about it.

jokes.text: Ron arrives and immediately starts to tell a story about Mayor Gunderson's dog. Leslie: 'Everybody stop talking until Justin gets here. Don't use up your stories.'
jokes.setup: Guests are arriving and naturally starting to socialize.
jokes.punchline: Leslie has apparently pre-approved a set of entertaining stories and is managing them as a finite resource, panicking that people will 'use up' their best material before Justin arrives.
jokes.explanation: Leslie treating dinner party conversation as a managed resource with scarcity concerns is perfectly insane and perfectly her. 'Don't use up your stories' is a great line that captures her controlling nature and her anxiety about the party in one phrase.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: First, I'm going to be the best Parks director this town has ever seen. Then I'm going to run for City Council. Then State Senate. Then Governor. Then President of the United States. And then, after I'm done being President, I'm going to write a mystery novel under a pseudonym and see if I can write a book that's so good that it wins the Pulitzer Prize.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And then I'm going to take that Pulitzer Prize, and I'm going to melt it down, and I'm going to recast it into a blimp. And I'm going to sail that blimp to the moon.

jokes.text: Ron continues trying to tell the dog story anyway. Leslie: 'What part of not talking do you not understand?'
jokes.setup: Leslie has just told everyone to stop talking and save their stories.
jokes.punchline: Ron immediately ignores this and continues the story, requiring Leslie to escalate.
jokes.explanation: A functional extension of joke 27. Ron's bulldozing through Leslie's instructions is a good character beat but not a new joke — it's more of a sustained comedic dynamic. Works in the room but doesn't add much beyond momentum.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Justin, I'm going to give you the most amazing night of your life. I know I always say that and then I don't deliver, but this time I really mean it. Actually, no, I'm definitely going to over-hype this and disappoint you, but that's not going to stop me from continuing to over-hype it anyway.

jokes.text: Leslie's wish list talking-head: 'build a new park from scratch... eventually become president... solve a murder on a train.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is explaining how much she wants this dinner party to succeed.
jokes.punchline: Her three deepest life ambitions are listed as equivalent: civic achievement, political aspiration, and solving a murder on a train — the last of which is a completely unexpected, specific, non-political fantasy.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and a genuine Parks and Rec classic. The list structure sets up two expected Leslie ambitions (park, presidency) and then delivers an absurdist non-sequitur that is somehow completely consistent with who she is — a romantic, adventure-loving bureaucrat who has watched too many Agatha Christie adaptations. 'Solve a murder on a train' as a sincere life goal is perfectly Leslie. Justified 8.7 — original, perfectly structured, deeply character-specific, beautifully economical, and completely earned.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Hi, I'm Ann. I have pancreatic cancer.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: She doesn't have pancreatic cancer.

jokes.text: Leslie tells Justin it's going to be 'the best, most exciting night of your life. I cannot over-hype it enough.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is welcoming Justin and promising a great party.
jokes.punchline: The meta-statement 'I cannot over-hype it enough' — meaning she's trying to hype it as much as humanly possible — is simultaneously self-aware and completely oblivious to how anxious she sounds.
jokes.explanation: The line is funny because 'I cannot over-hype it enough' implies maximum hype is the goal and that goal is unreachable — revealing Leslie's obsessive anxiety. It's a nice piece of character writing disguised as a throwaway line.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Whoa, that's a sweet coat. Where'd you get it?

dialogue.speaker: Justin
dialogue.line: Thanks! I got it in Cambodia.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Cambodia? That's awesome. I've always wanted to go there. What were you doing there?

dialogue.speaker: Justin
dialogue.line: I was climbing Mount Everest.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, Mount Everest is in Cambodia?

dialogue.speaker: Justin
dialogue.line: No, it's in Nepal.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So you were climbing Mount Everest in Nepal, but you bought the coat in Cambodia?

dialogue.speaker: Justin
dialogue.line: Yeah.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: That doesn't make any sense, dude.

jokes.text: Tom greets Justin with 'I have the swine flu.' Justin: 'Oh...' Leslie: 'No, she doesn't.'
jokes.setup: Tom is trying to impress Justin, but his opening gambit is claiming to have swine flu.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's matter-of-fact correction ('No, she doesn't') implies Tom tries this kind of weird attention-seeking regularly. The 'she' is also notable — unclear if Tom is being referred to as 'she' or if it's a script quirk.
jokes.explanation: A quick, weird character beat for Tom. The swine flu gambit is bizarre enough to land, and Leslie's weary correction ('No, she doesn't') suggests this is par for the course. The joke lives in the absurdity of Tom's strategy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Actually, no, I was being sarcastic. I would love that. That sounds amazing.

jokes.text: April considers putting gum in Justin's coat pockets. Andy declines out of loyalty to Leslie. April: 'I'll do it when you're not in the room then.' Andy: 'That would be terrible.' April: 'I'm being sarcastic. That would be awesome.'
jokes.setup: Andy and April are admiring Justin's coat and April suggests sabotaging it.
jokes.punchline: April's casual 'I'll do it when you're not in the room' followed by her correction of Andy's moral concern — her 'sarcasm' is that she actually does think it would be awesome — is a perfect April moment.
jokes.explanation: April's sarcasm-inversion ('I'm being sarcastic. That would be awesome.') is a great character beat — she uses the form of sarcasm while meaning the literal thing. This plants a seed that pays off later when gum actually ends up in the coat. Strong character integration for both characters.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh yeah, that mosque? I know the imam there. We go way back. He's like a brother to me.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: We text all the time. Just last week he sent me a picture of his new prayer rug. Very tasteful.

jokes.text: Tom admits to Justin that he barely knows India ('The last time I was in India I was eight years old and stayed inside playing video games') while scrambling to fact-check: 'Fourth largest coal reserves in the world.'
jokes.setup: Tom has been bonding with Justin over India, implying deep familiarity with the country.
jokes.punchline: His confessional reveals he's been faking it and is desperately researching while at the party. His only actual India fact: coal reserves.
jokes.explanation: The 'fourth largest coal reserves' as the only fact Tom can pull up while desperately Wikipedia-ing is both specific and perfectly Tom — always performing sophistication he doesn't have. The cut between his smooth party persona and his panicked fact-checking is excellent mockumentary structure.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You know, I actually know quite a bit about Indian culture. I've been studying it.

dialogue.speaker: Justin
dialogue.line: Oh really? Name one thing.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Um... curry. It's a thing they do there.

dialogue.speaker: Justin
dialogue.line: That's it?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Look, I'm gonna be honest with you. I know nothing about India. I just Googled 'India facts' five minutes ago and I'm still reading.

jokes.text: Andy's sarcasm clarification: 'I'm being sarcastic. That would be awesome.'
jokes.setup: Andy says the gum prank would be 'terrible' — then catches himself
jokes.punchline: Andy explicitly labels his previous statement as sarcasm and reverses his position: 'That would be awesome.'
jokes.explanation: Andy needing to clarify his own sarcasm — because he can't maintain the bit — is very Andy. The reversal is funny because it reveals he actually wanted to do the prank all along, which contradicts his earlier ethical stance. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Have you ever been to the Kaniman Mosque, down in Tamil Nadu? / Are you kidding? My uncle practically runs the place. I've prayed there. It's sick.
jokes.setup: Justin tests Tom's knowledge of South India; Tom admitted to knowing nothing.
jokes.punchline: Tom's immediate, confident, detailed lie — 'my uncle practically runs the place, I've prayed there, it's sick' — reveals he's now fully committed to faking Indian cultural knowledge.
jokes.explanation: Escalation of Tom's bluffing — he goes from 'the south part' to specific mosque knowledge with his uncle as a VIP. 'It's sick' is Tom's contemporary slang applied to a mosque, which is incongruous and funny. The escalation in one beat is well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Actually, that wasn't my story. That happened to a friend of mine.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: He's dead now, so he can't really tell you about it himself.

jokes.text: This is the best Old Fashioned I have ever had. Where'd you find this bartender? / Oh... I think... I don't know. Like, maybe the Yellow Pages. / There's no way that you're paying him enough.
jokes.setup: Justin raves about the bartender's cocktail.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's vague 'maybe the Yellow Pages' reveals the bartender is a rec center teacher demonstrating their class — and Justin's insistence they're underpaid makes it funnier.
jokes.explanation: Part of the running gag of rec center teachers performing at the party. Justin's rave review of a lobbying teacher is ironic. Functional but not especially sharp.

jokes.text: Leslie's attempt to 'casually' join Justin and Mark's conversation is immediately derailed — she starts describing a scenario where her 'face is literally on fire but it's a weird chemical so no one can see the flames.'
jokes.setup: Leslie wants to impress Justin but is visibly overwhelmed and anxious.
jokes.punchline: Her attempt at casual conversation produces an elaborate metaphor about invisible chemical face-fire, which is meant to convey anxiety but is so specific and strange it's its own comedy.
jokes.explanation: The invisible chemical fire is a surreal and specific anxiety metaphor that characterizes Leslie's overworked imagination. Slightly underdeveloped as a standalone joke but contributes to the mounting pressure of the party sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I wouldn't do that if I were you.

jokes.text: Justin tells a wild story about his face literally being on fire from a chemical, having to dunk it in sand. Then reveals: 'Didn't happen to me. It was a kid I knew from camp. But a great story's a great story.'
jokes.setup: Justin seems to be telling another of his incredible personal adventures, delivered with total authority.
jokes.punchline: It wasn't him. It was someone else. And Justin has apparently no problem presenting others' experiences as his own for storytelling purposes.
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural joke and a subtle character shift for Justin — he's not just worldly, he's apparently a fabulist. 'But a great story's a great story' is a perfectly delivered rationalization that gets a big laugh. This is the episode's first hint that Justin may be too good to be true, delivered as comedy. Rewatch bonus because you see it differently once you know his character.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So, did you know that Jerry's wife left him because he kept calling her by his ex-girlfriend's name? Anyway, how about those Colts?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh, and Donna told me in confidence that she's been taking salsa lessons, which I think is great for her self-esteem after her divorce. So what have you been up to?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom's been having some financial troubles, real money problems, but I'm sure he'd want you to know that. Want some snack mix?

jokes.text: 'Plus, the kid can't tell it. His mouth melted.'
jokes.setup: Justin has just justified telling someone else's story.
jokes.punchline: He adds that the original storyteller is unavailable to object — because his mouth melted from the chemical fire.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's strongest jokes. The casual, dark logic of 'his mouth melted' as a reason the kid can't reclaim his own story is brilliantly callous. Delivered deadpan, it transforms the previous joke into a dark comedy bit. Near-perfect economy — four words, enormous impact. The audience reaction in a group setting would be a shocked laugh, which is the best kind. Justified 8.4 craft score.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So... Derek seems nice.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: He is.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And he's very... tall.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, what are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm just saying, objectively, some people might find that attractive. Not me. I'm just saying statistically—

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: We're not doing this.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: —there's probably a demographic that—

jokes.text: A belly dancer shows up at the dinner party, apparently uninvited. Leslie: 'It's weird, but she just showed up.'
jokes.setup: The party has already gotten out of control with too many teachers showing up.
jokes.punchline: A belly dancer has also arrived, and Leslie maintains the fiction that it's a spontaneous occurrence.
jokes.explanation: A decent absurdist escalation of the 'teachers-as-entertainment' gag. The belly dancer is visually funny and Leslie's implausible denial is in character, but the joke itself is fairly thin.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I would describe it as a level nine on the pain scale. Which is the highest.

jokes.text: Tom is dared to eat a hot pepper from the soup. He accepts. He cries. Justin: 'You're very brave.' Tom, struggling: 'Please, that was one of the tiny ones.' Then Tom starts singing while suffering.
jokes.setup: A spicy pepper is at the table; Tom is challenged to eat it.
jokes.punchline: Tom eats it, is clearly in agony, but maintains his bravado ('that was one of the tiny ones') and then inexplicably starts singing, apparently as a coping mechanism.
jokes.explanation: Strong physical comedy beat. Tom's insistence on machismo while visibly suffering is perfect character comedy. The singing is unexpected and weird enough to be funny. 'That was one of the tiny ones' is a nice line.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, a belly dancer? What are the odds?

dialogue.speaker: Justin
dialogue.line: Leslie, you literally have the invoice in your hand.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm just as surprised as you are!

jokes.text: Tom trying to generate interesting party conversation introduces Derek and Ben as gay but mentions April 'on occasion will have relations with Derek.' Then: 'Discuss that.' Justin: 'There's not much more to discuss. You kind of explained it all.'
jokes.setup: Tom is trying to stir up interesting conversation at the party to keep Justin entertained.
jokes.punchline: Tom presents April's unusual relationship as a conversation starter, but his framing is so thorough that Justin correctly observes there's nothing left to discuss.
jokes.explanation: Justin's deadpan deflation of Tom's 'conversation starter' is well-timed. Tom oversharing April's personal life with a stranger and then saying 'discuss that' is perfectly Tom — he treats other people's relationships as entertainment content. Justin's dry response is the right punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This is incredible! A mariachi band, a juggler, AND a balloon artist all showed up to my party!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, you didn't hire these people?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No! They just... heard I was throwing a party and came. My reputation precedes me.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Your reputation for what? Wasting taxpayer money?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: For being fun, Ron. I'm a fun person. Entertainment gravitates toward me.

jokes.text: Justin's response to Tom's relationship expose: 'There's not much more to discuss. You kind of explained it all.'
jokes.setup: Tom has summarized April's romantic arrangement and commands the table to 'discuss'
jokes.punchline: Justin matter-of-factly notes there's nothing left to discuss because Tom summarized it completely
jokes.explanation: A clean deadpan button to the previous joke. Justin's response deflates Tom's gambit while also implying Justin is too worldly to be shocked by any of it. Functions well as a callback beat.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Yeah, Justin is awesome.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: He is pretty great. But remember, he's only 17, so we can't give him beer.

jokes.text: Tom's follow-up: 'Who else is gay?' after the conversation fails to launch.
jokes.setup: Tom's attempt at interesting conversation has fallen flat.
jokes.punchline: His solution is to prospect for more gay people to reveal, treating it as his party trick.
jokes.explanation: Economy is very strong — three words pivot from a failed joke into a new comedic direction. Tom's oblivious persistence is funny and consistent. Works well as a coda to the previous joke.

jokes.text: Leslie scolds Tom: 'Tom, I need your help. There was a lull. I saw Justin yawn. Please tell me that yawning is a sign of excitement in India or something.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is panicking that Justin is bored.
jokes.punchline: Her desperate hope that yawning might mean something different in India is both absurd and perfectly Leslie — she'd rather invent cross-cultural miscommunication than accept that the party is failing.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's escalating desperation produces a great absurdist rationalization. 'Please tell me yawning is a sign of excitement in India or something' is a wonderful character line — only Leslie would go there. The 'or something' trails off perfectly. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I would totally defend Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: But let's be honest, she's not the sharpest tool in the shed. She's more like... a shovel. A well-meaning shovel, but a shovel.

jokes.text: Ron: 'Poor Tommy. He has a very frail colon.' to Justin, out of nowhere.
jokes.setup: Tom has been gone a long time in the bathroom after eating the hot pepper.
jokes.punchline: Ron delivers a completely unnecessary and overly clinical update on Tom's digestive health to Justin, with total authority and no embarrassment.
jokes.explanation: Pure Ron Swanson. The clinical specificity of 'frail colon' delivered with zero irony or embarrassment is quintessential character comedy. Ron would state this fact to a near-stranger because it's factual and relevant — social filters simply don't apply. Great economy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm sorry. I feel like a dog who chewed up your favorite shoe.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It's okay.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, I feel like a monkey who stole your wallet.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Leslie, you don't have to—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I feel like a snake. A big, dumb snake that ruined your life.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, now you're just being racist.

jokes.text: Leslie's talking-head: 'People hear about a killer party at Knope's house, they all come running.'
jokes.setup: The party has been crashed by a belly dancer and various rec center teachers.
jokes.punchline: Leslie reframes the chaotic, obviously engineered party as organically legendary.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's self-mythologizing confessionals are a staple of the show's comedy. This is a solid example — her earnest belief in the party's organic cool is funny because we know she orchestrated all of it. Good character integration but not a particularly original construction.

dialogue.speaker: Questioner
dialogue.line: Where were you on the night of March 15th?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Where were you?

dialogue.speaker: Questioner
dialogue.line: I'm asking the questions here. Did you meet with the contractor?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Did you?

dialogue.speaker: Questioner
dialogue.line: Ron, please just answer directly. What did you discuss?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: What did you?

dialogue.speaker: Questioner
dialogue.line: This is a formal hearing!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Is it?

jokes.text: April's talking-head: 'You don't do origami every day, do ya?' followed by her confessional about the belly dancer: 'They brought in a little entertainment, thank God. That Justin, he's so boring.'
jokes.setup: The party has a belly dancer performing; April is watching.
jokes.punchline: April's entire evaluation of Justin — who the rest of the party finds fascinating — is that he's boring, which says more about April than Justin.
jokes.explanation: April's contrarianism is well-deployed here. Her boredom with the universally admired Justin is consistent characterization. 'Thank God' for the belly dancer is a nice deadpan moment.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Betrayment. That's what this is. Pure betrayment.

jokes.text: Andy cuts off a young-looking guest who wants a drink: 'You're underage. I could lose my liquor license, I'm sorry.'
jokes.setup: The party is getting chaotic; various guests are mingling.
jokes.punchline: Andy, who is working as a coat-check and is not running a licensed bar, invokes a liquor license he definitely does not have.
jokes.explanation: A nice bit of Andy taking his coat-check duties very seriously and expanding his self-perceived authority. 'I could lose my liquor license' when he has no such thing is funny because it reveals Andy constructing a professional identity in real time.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, so Justin didn't betray Leslie? That's great! I feel so much better. I'm gonna go un-say all the mean things I said about him. I'm gonna say... the opposite things.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Justin, you're the worst! No wait, un-worst. You're the... best-ish.

jokes.text: An accountant crashes the party demanding an evaluation of his class. His opening: 'When it comes to choosing accounting software, there's no accounting for taste.' He laughs alone.
jokes.setup: Another teacher has crashed the party to lobby for their class.
jokes.punchline: His icebreaker is an accounting pun he finds hilarious; no one else does.
jokes.explanation: The pun itself ('no accounting for taste') is a tired one, but the joke is really about his delighted solo laughter in a room of cold silence — that's the cringe comedy. The accountant's oblivious enthusiasm is the actual punchline. Works as a type-character moment.

dialogue.speaker: Justin
dialogue.line: The party was amazing. Leslie planned everything perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Your Honor, I rest my case. Also, I love you.

jokes.text: 'When it comes to choosing accounting software, there's no accounting for taste.' (Teacher laughs at his own joke.)
jokes.setup: The accounting teacher arrives and announces he wants an evaluation
jokes.punchline: He delivers a pun about accounting software / 'no accounting for taste,' then laughs appreciatively at his own joke
jokes.explanation: A deliberately bad pun — the meta-joke is that this person thinks this is his best material and laughs at it himself. The pun is genuinely weak (that's intentional), but the comedy shifts to cringe when he laughs. Works as character comedy for a nerdy, oblivious instructor. The fact that it's intentionally bad limits the craft score but the cringe layer saves it from a 3.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Because I'm in love with you, Ann. And I wanted to do this officially, in front of the Parks and Recreation Advisory Board. This is the most important thing I've ever done.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, what are you talking about?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann Perkins, will you be my best friend? I already have the legal documents drawn up. Once you sign these papers, our friendship will be legally binding, and if you ever want to break up with me, you'll have to go through a lengthy custody battle over our shared friends.

jokes.text: Ron: 'Well, this is great. I'm heading home, so as not to have to be here anymore.'
jokes.setup: The accounting teacher begins a 45-minute QuickBooks presentation.
jokes.punchline: Ron's reason for leaving is stated with perfect clarity and zero social grace: he is leaving specifically to avoid continuing to be present.
jokes.explanation: A candidate for the episode's best one-liner. Ron's reason for leaving — phrased as 'so as not to have to be here anymore' — is simultaneously the most honest and least socially acceptable exit statement possible. The formal grammatical construction ('so as not to') combined with the blunt content is perfectly Ron. Genuinely excellent writing. Justified 8.3 craft and 8.5 impact.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I don't care about actually helping people. I just want the government to tell me I'm doing a good job.

jokes.text: Tom at the hearing: 'I would like to say that Leslie is incapable of using people for her own gain. Thank you, Tom. But I can't, because Leslie loves using people for her own gain.'
jokes.setup: Tom appears to be preparing to defend Leslie at her hearing.
jokes.punchline: He pivots immediately to accurately and enthusiastically confirming her guilt, having set up the defense only to knock it down.
jokes.explanation: Excellent structure — the joke is built on the classic 'set up the defense and immediately withdraw it' construction, but Tom pre-thanks himself for his own testimony ('Thank you, Tom') before undermining it. That self-congratulatory middle beat is what elevates this above a standard pivot joke. The rhythm is perfect. Justified 8.2 craft score — this is sharp, well-constructed comedy writing.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Justin, you are a true entrepreneur. You've built an empire from nothing. You're living the dream.

dialogue.speaker: Justin
dialogue.line: Tom, I appreciate that, but didn't you just spend the last twenty minutes complaining about how much you hate working?

jokes.text: I would like to say that Leslie is incapable of using people for her own gain. / Thank you, Tom. / But I can't, because Leslie loves using people for her own gain.
jokes.setup: Tom appears to be delivering a character defense of Leslie at the disciplinary hearing.
jokes.punchline: The classic double-negative structure — 'I would like to say X... but I can't, because Y' — delivers the opposite of the expected defense.
jokes.explanation: A structurally clean joke. The 'I would like to say... but I can't' form is a well-worn comic structure, but it's executed with good rhythm here. Tom's inability to actually defend Leslie despite wanting to is funny and character-appropriate.

jokes.text: Leslie's apology to Tom for inviting Wendy escalates: 'I put a beautiful man in front of an adorable man-child.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is apologizing to Tom for prioritizing Justin over their friendship.
jokes.punchline: Her metaphors escalate in specificity and become progressively more insulting to Tom, culminating in 'adorable man-child.'
jokes.explanation: 'Adorable man-child' is a memorable characterization of Tom. Leslie's apology being itself a series of escalating insults is funny because she's completely unaware of the damage she's doing while trying to repair it. Good escalation structure.

jokes.text: Leslie extends the metaphor: 'I put a big white stallion in front of a little brown pony.' Tom: 'Totally uncalled for.'
jokes.setup: Leslie's apology has already insulted Tom with 'adorable man-child.'
jokes.punchline: She escalates to a horse metaphor that's both racially coded and physically diminishing. Tom's 'totally uncalled for' is the perfect dry protest.
jokes.explanation: The horse metaphor escalation is the peak of this running joke. The 'little brown pony' is a step too far in exactly the right direction, and Tom's measured 'totally uncalled for' is funnier than any bigger reaction would be. The joke earns its racially-tinged edge because it's clearly about Leslie's obliviousness, not malice. Good escalation payoff.

jokes.text: Ron's talking-head about his hearing strategy: 'The only type of witness I enjoy being is a hostile one. That's why I intend to answer every one of their questions with a question.'
jokes.setup: Ron is about to testify at Leslie's disciplinary hearing.
jokes.punchline: Ron has pre-committed to being maximally obstructive at an official proceeding, treating hostile witness behavior as a preferred mode rather than a last resort.
jokes.explanation: Ron's philosophy of governance distilled into testimony strategy. 'The only type of witness I enjoy being is a hostile one' is a perfect Ron Swanson line — it captures his libertarian contempt for institutional proceedings while revealing a surprising strategic mind. High quotability. Justified 8.1 — this is character-defining comedy writing.

jokes.text: Ron's testimony sequence: answers every question with a question. 'Would I have stayed if I knew that?' / 'I don't know, would you have?' / 'Would you have?' / 'No. I wouldn't have.'
jokes.setup: Ron has announced his intention to answer every question with a question.
jokes.punchline: He executes the plan, forcing the committee member into the spiral, until Ron himself accidentally answers directly ('No. I wouldn't have.'), breaking his own rule.
jokes.explanation: The payoff for Ron's strategy setup is superb. The escalating question spiral is perfectly structured, and Ron accidentally breaking his own rule by answering directly is the unexpected twist that elevates the joke. The committee member being drawn into Ron's game ('I don't know, would you have?') shows the joke has momentum. Justified 8.5 — this is excellent sitcom comedy construction, making good on a setup with a structurally satisfying payoff.

jokes.text: Ron asks if the committee member knows Latin after 'quid pro quo' is mentioned. Committee: 'Okay, thank you, Ron.' Ron: 'Are we done? Can I get a shine?'
jokes.setup: Ron's testimony is wrapping up.
jokes.punchline: Ron pivots immediately from government testimony to requesting a shoe shine, treating the entire official proceeding as a minor interruption to his day.
jokes.explanation: Ron asking for a shoe shine upon conclusion of official government testimony is perfectly in character — he's there, Andy presumably is nearby, efficiency demands multi-tasking. The character logic is airtight and the request is delivered as a completely reasonable next step.

jokes.text: Andy: 'I'm sorry. But I don't know what you're talking about. Why don't you ask your new best friend, Justin?' — then reveals he put gum in Justin's coat, calling it 'unbetrayed'
jokes.setup: Andy is upset with Leslie; when she apologizes, he's cold — until he reveals the gum prank actually happened
jokes.punchline: Justin 'is probably too busy cleaning gum out of his coat pockets.' Andy declares himself 'unbetrayed.'
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback payoff. Andy went through with the prank after all, and his coinage 'unbetrayed' as a single word capturing his restored sense of dignity is a great Andy-ism. The joke rewards attentive viewers who remembered the earlier setup. 'Unbetrayed' is a minor verbal gem — the kind of malapropism/neologism that feels authentic to the character.

jokes.text: Andy reveals someone put gum in Justin's coat pockets. 'But he's probably too busy cleaning gum out of his coat pockets.' Ron: 'Wow. Unbetrayed.'
jokes.setup: Andy had refused to put gum in Justin's pockets out of loyalty to Leslie. April had threatened to do it anyway.
jokes.punchline: The gum is in the pockets, vindicating Andy's earlier loyalty while the perpetrator (April, presumably) executed the plan. Ron's 'Unbetrayed' is a perfect coinage — the reversal of Andy's 'betrayment.'
jokes.explanation: A multi-layered callback that pays off two earlier jokes simultaneously: April's gum threat and Andy's 'betrayment.' Ron's coinage of 'Unbetrayed' — matching Andy's fake word with a fake antonym — is genuinely brilliant, suggesting Ron absorbed Andy's malapropism and deployed it back perfectly. The emotional resolution (Andy feels vindicated, their friendship restored) is handled through wordplay. This is exactly the kind of payoff that earns its 8+ scores.

jokes.text: Leslie explains why she turned herself in: 'It's every girl's dream to ask a dude how their date went under penalty of perjury.'
jokes.setup: Ann is confused about why Leslie voluntarily requested the disciplinary hearing.
jokes.punchline: Leslie reveals she engineered the entire hearing as an elaborate way to officially depose Justin about whether he had a good time on their date — treating a government proceeding as a relationship-confirmation tool.
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke and one of the best Leslie Knope jokes in the series. The revelation recontextualizes the entire hearing scene and is completely, perfectly in character — of course Leslie Knope would weaponize a government disciplinary proceeding to get official confirmation that her date went well. 'Under penalty of perjury' as a relationship communication tool is both absurdist and deeply true to who she is. The line is immediately quotable, the setup across the entire episode is earned, and the character integration is 10/10 — this joke could ONLY be Leslie Knope. Justified 9.1 craft — this approaches the caliber of 'Snip, snap!' in terms of character-defining comedy writing.

jokes.text: Leslie adds: 'The most important thing is, there is now an official government document that proves my dinner party kicked ass.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has just explained her self-serving use of the hearing.
jokes.punchline: She identifies the hearing's true value: an official permanent record of the party's quality, certified by the government.
jokes.explanation: The perfect coda to the episode's central joke. Leslie having weaponized government infrastructure to certify her party's quality is both absurd and deeply consistent. 'Proves my dinner party kicked ass' as official government documentation is a wonderful phrase. The joke earns every bit of its high score because it's the culmination of everything the episode has built.

jokes.text: Tom to Justin: 'I'm not gay, but you're the most incredible man I've ever met.' Justin: 'That doesn't sound gay at all.'
jokes.setup: Tom is wrapping up his conversation with Justin and makes a declaration of admiration.
jokes.punchline: Justin deadpans that Tom's emphatic disclaimer has done nothing to make the statement sound less gay.
jokes.explanation: A clean ironic callback joke — the denial making the thing more true is a classic structure. Justin's dry 'that doesn't sound gay at all' is well-timed. Not the most original construction but executed cleanly.

tmdb_overview: After an amazing date with Justin in Indianapolis, Leslie tries to impress him with a dinner party at her house.
insight: Solid character work carries a quieter episode with steady mid-range laughs and no peak moments.
